title: Norton v. Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance
lead: Environmental organizations seek judicial orders to protect Utah land from off-road vehicles. Each requested order must be traced to a specific unfinished act that the law actually requires.

actors.name: Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance and other environmental organizations
actors.role: Collectively SUWA; challenged BLM’s response to off-road-vehicle use.

actors.name: Bureau of Land Management
actors.role: Federal agency managing the Utah lands and preparing the land-use plans.

actors.name: Secretary of the Interior and other federal officials
actors.role: Defended the agency and sought Supreme Court review.

proceedings: SUWA sued in federal district court in 1999; the court dismissed the three challenged categories of inaction.
A divided Tenth Circuit revived the relevant claims.
The Supreme Court unanimously reversed and remanded on June 14, 2004.
limits: This account follows the source brief’s historical 2004 law and assigned editorial material, without a new audit or current-law certification. The Court did not determine whether all alleged environmental injuries occurred or approve every BLM management practice. Completed planning steps became moot; the surviving monitoring claim failed for lack of a binding duty, with discreteness expressly reserved.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with the complete effective canonical brief; no new independent opinion verification claimed.

sections.title: BLM manages land while Congress considers wilderness protection
sections.cue: What was protected, and what did SUWA say was happening?
paragraphs: The Bureau of Land Management (BLM) managed nearly 23 million acres of federal land in Utah. The Federal Land Policy and Management Act of 1976 (FLPMA) directed management for multiple use and sustained yield and required land-use planning. BLM also identified wilderness study areas for Congress to consider designating as wilderness. Study status did not automatically impose every restriction applicable to congressionally designated wilderness.

Under FLPMA § 1782(c), BLM had to manage study areas without impairing their suitability for preservation as wilderness, subject to the statute’s qualifications. That obligation continued pending Congress’s decision even for areas the Secretary had not recommended for wilderness designation. Off-road vehicles were allowed on parts of the affected land. Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance and other environmental organizations, collectively SUWA, alleged that increasing vehicle use threatened wilderness characteristics. The allegation supplied the controversy; the Supreme Court did not find every claimed injury established.

BLM’s broad plans described future, more specific work. The San Rafael plan covered about 1.5 million acres and twenty resource-management categories, including projected vehicle-route work. The Henry Mountains plan described use supervision and monitoring. Those statements later became possible sources of the duties SUWA wanted enforced.

sources.pinpoint: Material facts and statutory framework; 542 U.S. 58–61, 69–71

sections.title: SUWA brings three demands to the district court
sections.cue: What act did each theory ask the court to compel?
paragraphs: In 1999 SUWA sued federal officials under Administrative Procedure Act (APA) § 706(1), which permits courts to compel agency action unlawfully withheld or unreasonably delayed. First, SUWA alleged that BLM had failed to protect wilderness study areas from impairment by vehicles. Second, it alleged that BLM had failed to carry out commitments in its land-use plans, including a San Rafael route-designation plan and Henry Mountains supervision and monitoring. Third, it sought further environmental analysis under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) because vehicle use had increased.

The federal district court dismissed the three claims. A divided Tenth Circuit reversed in relevant part. The appellate court treated the alleged failure to prevent impairment as reviewable inaction, viewed plan implementation as enforceable, and concluded that the agency had to take a hard look at new information bearing on environmental supplementation. The Secretary of the Interior and other officials obtained Supreme Court review. The Court heard argument on March 29, 2004.

Agency work during the litigation narrowed the controversy. BLM completed the San Rafael route-designation plan and established use-supervision files for designated Henry Mountains areas, making demands for those steps moot to that extent. A Factory Butte continuing-monitoring demand remained live even though a program had recently begun: starting a program did not resolve a claim seeking its continued implementation. The Supreme Court addressed that surviving demand and indicated that the same reasoning would govern any asserted continuing-maintenance duty.

sections.title: The Supreme Court identifies two limits on an order to act
sections.cue: Why are specificity and legal obligation separate requirements?
paragraphs: Justice Scalia wrote for a unanimous Court. APA § 551(13) defines agency action through identifiable acts—rules, orders, licenses, sanctions and relief—along with equivalents, denials and failures to act. Reading the residual terms in that setting, the Court required a sufficiently circumscribed omitted action. A denial is a decision refusing relief; a failure to act can be the omission of a required response. Calling a general management deficiency a failure did not identify the particular action missing.

Section 706(1) also carried forward mandamus-like limits: the act must be legally obligatory. Unreasonable delay did not avoid that requirement, because an agency cannot unlawfully delay an act it has no duty to perform. Discretion about content was different from freedom not to act at all. If a statute required regulations by a deadline, a court could compel their issuance while leaving their permissible content to the agency.

The resulting rule required a discrete action that the agency was legally required to take. Consistent with Lujan v. National Wildlife Federation’s rejection of broad programmatic attacks, courts could not use the APA to assume administration of an entire program. A general compliance decree would force continuing judicial decisions about priorities, resources and implementation. The Court did not immunize all inaction; it restricted this action-forcing remedy to specific obligatory acts.

sections.title: The nonimpairment objective leaves BLM a choice of means
sections.cue: Why did a mandatory objective fail to support SUWA’s broad compliance order?
paragraphs: FLPMA’s nonimpairment command imposed a real management objective, but it did not specify the particular protective measures SUWA wanted. BLM retained discretion to choose among ways of protecting wilderness suitability. Treating that broad goal as an order to undertake measures selected by the plaintiffs would transfer the selection of means to a court.

A decree requiring general compliance would also place everyday land-management choices under continuing judicial supervision. The Court rejected that approach under § 706(1). It did not hold that BLM had no substantive duties, that off-road use caused no harm, or that all management choices were lawful. This claim failed because the broad objective did not identify a discrete act that BLM was required to perform.

sections.title: Plan conformity does not make every future project compulsory
sections.cue: Why did the surviving monitoring demand fail without deciding discreteness?
paragraphs: SUWA next relied on § 1732(a), requiring management in accordance with land-use plans. The Court accepted that a plan could constrain later action: a specific inconsistent implementation decision could support a § 706(2) challenge. It rejected the inference that every projected future activity thereby became an affirmative duty enforceable under § 706(1).

The regulations treated plans as frameworks guiding future management and more detailed planning, ordinarily distinct from final implementation decisions requiring further process. Plan approval could be protested to the BLM director, while specific implementation decisions followed a different administrative appeal route. That distinction supported reading plans as guidance rather than exhaustive lists of immediately compulsory actions.

The San Rafael plan projected work involving routes, grazing, habitat, fire, recreation, cultural resources and watersheds over several years. Making every projected step compulsory could commit money not yet appropriated and displace more urgent priorities. In that context, the Court read the Henry Mountains supervision-and-monitoring language as qualified by budgets and priorities even where every qualification was not express.

A plan could reiterate a duty independently imposed by law or use language creating a binding commitment. These particular statements did neither. The surviving monitoring claim therefore failed for lack of a binding duty; the Court expressly did not decide whether the requested monitoring was discrete. Footnote 5 also reserved a possible claim under a regulation specifically addressing monitoring, because that was not the claim before the Court. The holding did not make every monitoring obligation unenforceable.

sections.title: Completed plan approval defeats this supplementation theory
sections.cue: What remained of the NEPA claim, and what did the final judgment do?
paragraphs: NEPA required environmental analysis for qualifying major federal action. The regulation at issue required supplementation for significant new circumstances or information bearing on that action or its effects. Marsh v. Oregon Natural Resources Council required a hard look at new information while major federal action remained underway; the dam construction in Marsh had not been completed.

Here the relevant federal action was approval of the land-use plan, and approval was complete. The plan’s continuing existence did not turn its approval into an ongoing action. Later information about vehicle use therefore did not trigger the asserted supplementation duty on this theory. An amendment or revision could require additional NEPA analysis. The result depended on what the federal action was and whether it remained unfinished, rather than on a universal exemption for land management.

On June 14, 2004, the Supreme Court reversed the Tenth Circuit and remanded. No routes were ordered closed, no judicial monitoring program was imposed, and no requested supplemental analysis was ordered. There were no Supreme Court concurrences or dissents; the earlier division was in the Tenth Circuit. The three theories had distinct outcomes: broad nonimpairment lacked the required discrete act, surviving plan monitoring lacked a binding affirmative duty, and NEPA supplementation lacked a remaining major federal action. The completed plan-preparation demands had become moot, not lost on their merits.

The assigned editorial aftermath describes subsequent lower-court dismissals, connects Norton to Ohio Forestry, and discusses the Forest Service’s 2005 strategic-planning rule and 2006 categorical exclusions. Those are historical editorial accounts, citing Perch-Ahern, Blumm and Bosse, and the relevant Federal Register notices. They add no Norton holding and do not establish the current validity of those later rules. The source brief compared the historical opinion and assigned pages; it does not claim a complete review of the cited articles or later rulemaking records.
